utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We are a full house today. The accused, Defence and Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. Witness is already in the courtroom. I think Mr. Bourgon can proceed. You don't have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I was done, Mr. President. Mr. Meek was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was under the impression that you still had a couple of questions. All right so it's Mr. Meek to be followed by Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, how are you today, sir?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Very briefly, yesterday when we were finishing up, you had mentioned that -- this would be at line -- page 73, line 17 through 20, that: "On the 12th, in the evening, and on the 13th, in the evening, they were ambushed during the night on the 12th, we received an order to be prepared that afternoon. And they should be sent during the night into Tisova Kosa sector." Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And were you referring to -- just tell the Chamber who you were referring to on those two nights and the ambushes.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That ambush was sent to the sector of Tisova Kosa in case of an attack by the Muslim forces from the area of Srebrenica, in order to protect the defence line of our battalion from the back. That order had arrived from the brigade, because along that axis, both in 1992 and in 1993, certain groups from Srebrenica used to pass in the direction of Tuzla and this also repeated in March 1993. That axis was used by some 300 soldiers and civilians to access Tuzla from the direction of Srebrenica. That is why those ambushes were set up, in order to protect the front line of our defence from the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware during that period of time any ambushes which did take place? And I believe yesterday you did mention ambushes taking place with Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from the brigade that during that period of time, during the 12th and the 13th, Major Obrenovic went to intercept the column, setting up a sort of an ambush. I don't know what his intention was. I suppose it was to prevent the break through of these groups towards Zvornik, towards the surrounding villages, and I know that he asked for the intervention unit on the 13th in order to reinforce his troops in the Snagovo sector. That's how I realised that there was a large group, a long column of people that had to be intercepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ristic, do you recall receiving a commendation shortly after these events?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that it was somewhere in the newspapers after the events in the Drina Corps, I was commended by the brigade commander for good comport, something to that effect, something that had to do with the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And are you aware that in that commendation, not only you but other units were commended, among other things, upon inflicting enormous losses on the enemy during that time period? Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly but I know that I wasn't alone to be commended. I believe that the commanders of the 6th Battalion, the 7th Battalion were also mentioned. I don't know which other units were also mentioned. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. You're correct. It wasn't just you and the 4th Battalion but you do understand, Mr. Ristic, that among other things, the commendation was for inflicting great losses on the enemy, correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I understood the commendation, it was bestowed as a result of combat activities and the things that happened in the sector of my battalion during those days. I believe that it had to do with the fighting. I don't know the exact wording of the commendation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Ristic, during the period of time from 1992 to 1995, when you were in the intelligence/security sector, you had a dual role; is that correct, both as security and intelligence?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could you enlighten me and just tell me what the difference is between intelligence, what their duties would be, as opposed to security?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intelligence duties were about the enemy situation, and counterintelligence had to do with the work of the unit within the unit where I was, that is the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And can you enlighten me and the Chamber what would be the duties for security, as opposed to the intelligence?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the difference lies in the fact that the intelligence activity of the assistant commander in the battalion consists in the reporting to the commander of the brigade about the positions of the enemy troops, and the security situation in the battalion concerns the work of the battalion, destructive activities, running away from the positions, and this was also reported to the military police in agreement with the commander of the battalion. If the infringement was of a lesser magnitude, then it could be reported to the commander of the battalion. If it was more serious, then to the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ristic, during that period of time, which we are talking about, from 1992 to 1995, could you -- March of 1995, when you took over some command responsibilities as you testified to, can you tell me approximately what percentage of the time you would spend on intelligence work as opposed to security work?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the period while I was assistant commander of the battalion, you mean? Or throughout the entire period?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, sir. Let me -- it's my understanding that from 1992 to approximately March of 1995, you were in the security and intelligence sector and in fact you just answered that a little bit earlier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So my question was, before you went to the command or assistant commander of the battalion in March of 1995, what percentage, approximately, did you spend on security matters as opposed to intelligence matters?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you any ratios concerning that part of my job. But the everyday task of the assistant commander for intelligence was to monitor through the company commanders, men on the lines and in the trenches, to monitor the movement of the enemy. That was an everyday task. In agreement with company commanders, if there was a problem with the troops in the companies, everything went through company commanders who would address the assistant commander for security. That was my everyday job and it's very hard for me to talk about any ratios.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I can appreciate that and I want to clarify one thing. I think I earlier misspoke when I said from March of 1992 to March of 1995. It was actually March of 1993 to March of 1995. Is that correct, Mr. Ristic, when you were in that position in the sector of security and intelligence?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Ristic, I just have one other issue I'd like to ask you about. Do you recall giving an interview to -- with Mr. McCloskey from the Office of the Prosecutor, back in 2004? April 8, 2004.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. At the end of that, Mr. McCloskey asked you if you had any complaints and you said no, that you were satisfied. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, you went on to say, though, that you really wouldn't like to participate in this because you believe that during that period it was not a normal situation which you were engaged in, it was a war, and you were a person who was living off your work and you believe that you didn't hurt anyone during this war, even on the Muslim side. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall telling Mr. McCloskey then that in regards to the Muslims at that time, that they were your neighbours and that they are still your neighbours, that they came back and that "we live in sort of a normal surrounding and we are all surviving"? Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And again, having been that interview a few years back, is it a fair statement that the Muslims have returned to the villages where you came from and life is getting back to normal?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Meek. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, I don't want to go over old ground with you, but I want to clarify one or two matters to do with dates. When you began your evidence two days ago, at page 10043 of the transcript, you described how on the 12th of July, you received a telegram from the brigade instructing to you form a platoon out of companies. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You then talked about the 13th of July and said that you were informed from the brigade that a platoon was coming to your aid, a platoon from the 3rd Infantry Battalion and they were supposed to provide security support for the mortar platoon. Do you recall that as well, don't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The reason I've asked to you clarify that is because, at page 10093 of the transcript, when you were initially being asked questions by my learned friend Mr. Bourgon for Drago Nikolic, he suggested to you, I suspect inadvertently that the events in relation to the intervention squad had taken place on the 14th of July. It had in fact taken place on the 13th of July as you initially said. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, that intervention platoon of the battalion arrived in the area of Tisova Kosa and Grujica Brdo and on the 14th in the morning it was dispatched to the Snagovo sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you remember when on the 13th of July it arrived?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was around noon. During that period of time, around noon or maybe early in the afternoon. We had ample time to inspect the line, to talk. It was daylight. I'm sure that it was in the afternoon on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when were you first informed on the 13th of July that it would in fact be arriving?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the intervention platoon of the 3rd Infantry Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do mean that, yes.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the period of time when they were sent towards me, I had been informed by the brigade that the 3rd -- actually, the intervention platoon of the 3rd Infantry Battalion was on its way to the Grujica Brdo area and they asked me to deploy them. During that period of time, maybe half an hour before their arrival, I had been informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So sometime in the late morning, perhaps, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, by this time, and let's use this as a convenient point in time, the point that you had been informed of the arrival of the intervention platoon, you were aware of an imminent military threat from the column; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And by that time, you had taken initial steps to try and detect and block the column, correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that Major Obrenovic had gone to the area of Snagovo to intercept that column. We were preparing some sort of defence because there was a possibility that they might attack us as well and this is all I knew at the time about the column and about the developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That will suffice for my purposes. Apart from the fear that they might attack you, there was a fear that they might attack surrounding Serb villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In short, you were being put on the maximum level of alert and full combat readiness, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And as I think you've already described, you had a particular fear that some of the men in the column might suddenly attack your rear, correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yesterday, when you were being asked questions by my learned friend Mr. Haynes for Vinko Pandurevic, you confirmed that you were able to see the military aspect of this column quite well on the 17th of July; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you saw with your own eyes that it was in fact, as far as you were concerned, well armed and well organised?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I saw a column of civilians. It was a very, very long column walking, and there were women and men in that column. I didn't pay too much attention to the fact whether they all had arms but some did. I was standing at a distance of some 500 metres and I could see the column very well. It was between 10 and 20 metres wide. It was very long. It was passing. It had 24 hours to pass. Once our line was closed, there were still some groups that managed to go through and they kept on passing. When we went to inspect that part where they were passing, we saw that the grass, which had been high, was lying low and you could actually see the soil. The soil had been trampled on, the grass had been trampled on which means that quite a lot of Muslim population had passed through.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And specifically, it's the military aspect that I wanted to ask you about. You had mentioned that one of your men had counted 32 84-millimetre machine-guns. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the 17th, in the afternoon, when we were supposed to bring our lines up to manpower level, and that was near our command which had burnt down. I saw that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And intermingled were -- with those guns were a lot of uniformed soldiers, and as far as you could see, this column did pose the threat that you had prepared for back on the 13th of July; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was our practice, as I said, in 1993, a number of civilians passed through our line of defence in the following manner. Some armed men went before and after them, and in a manner of speaking they pierced our line of defence and passed through. And we assumed that they would do the same now. And this proved to be so. They attacked us. We had to leave our command post. They had weapons. And in that period we had 11 killed and one missing. He was never found. We had 20 wounded. That was how the fighting happened in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I just want to you confirm that in addition to the men and arms that you have described being present in the column, the column also had artillery support. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Artillery support came from the direction of Nezuk. They were firing upon the command post. Someone was probably telling them where to fire. So those on that side and those from the 2nd Corps had communication probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have -- yesterday, you said that you would have a few questions on redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you, Your Honours and counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ristic. I think just now you just indicated on questioning by Mr. Josse, my learned friend there, on the 13th when you were informed of the intervention platoon from the 3rd Battalion being on its way that you were on maximum alert because of what you perceived to be an imminent danger; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the highest level of alert. We were on alert for a possible attack every day. According to our previous experience, in Baljkovica, we had to be alert and prepared for an attack because we did not have information as to the movements of those people. We didn't know exactly when they would arrive in our area so we had to be alert in every respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for interrupting but this has to do with the interpretation of the witness's reply. The transcript does not reflect what the witness said in B/C/S. Perhaps the witness did not enunciate the word clearly. Could this be clarified? I think the witness said it was not the highest level of alert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 19 on page 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you could address it yourself, Mr. Vanderpuye. But in answering your question, the very first statement of the witness is, "That was the highest level of alert." And we are being told that he didn't say so, so perhaps you could address it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, I think you probably have understood the concerns of the president and also my learned friend. Could you tell us, with respect to the level of alert that you had on that day, I guess that would be on the 13th of July, could you tell us was that the maximum level or not the maximum level?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the maximum level. It was only a higher level of alert. Because we did not ask for assistance. Had it been the maximum level we would probably have asked for assistance to defend the command post and the line. We did not have information as to what kind of group this was. We did not ask for assistance but we were more alert than usual in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to then clarify, in response to the question that was put to you by my learned friend Mr. Josse, I think it's at page 9, lines 6 through 8 in the transcript, he asked you in short were you being put on the maximum level of alert and full combat readiness, weren't you? And your answer was yes. Does your response now change your response to his question that was put to you earlier as well?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably didn't understand properly but I have just explained in my previous answer what the level of alert was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So would it be fair to say that the level of alert that were you on was a heightened level of alert, higher than normal?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A greater level of alertness and caution was required. The company commanders had to cooperate. Also the commander of the mortar platoon. People were not allowed to leave their posts. Everyone had to be ready for a possible attack, to be ready to fire from their position that they were assigned to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And during this period of time, did you make any effort to recall any of the personnel that you had released prior to this state of readiness or alertness?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this period, I called a colleague from the battalion, whom I had allowed to go, to go away for a certain period, to deal with some business. He had been absent for seven days. I didn't have a battalion commander. This man was familiar with the situation. He had been a company leader for some time and I called him asked him to come and help me and he did, and he went to the ambush with those men and unfortunately he was killed on the 15th -- no, on the 16th of July, near the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, I just wanted to take you to a couple of different areas, two different areas specifically. The first has to do with some questions that were put to you by my learned friend Mr. Haynes regarding an order, a 1993 order, that was apparently issued by Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, and in particular, I think you were asked to read the last paragraph of that answer -- of that order. Do you recall having done that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I have please P02504 displayed in e-court? Could I have, Madam Usher, could I have the order itself actually physically handed to the witness? I don't believe I can display both simultaneously in e-court, can I? It's 7D0036. I have it here in my hand, if you could hand it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could just refer to you the last paragraph? Okay, Mr. Ristic, do you recall having read that yesterday into the record?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what you read in the record, is it page 10162, line 21 through 10163, line 4, that: "Armed groups should be considered terrorists because recently they have inflicted major losses on us, in case of the groups passing and being blocked and in case they finally lay their arms, and if there are unarmed persons and civilians among them, make sure they are treated as prisoners honouring and complying with international conventions on their protection." Now, with respect to that particular, as a deputy commander, battalion commander, reading that latter part of the order, what is your understanding regarding armed groups should be treated or should be considered terrorists? With respect to the B/C/S version it would be the last page. I think it's page 3.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For us in the battalion, all these armed groups were considered to be enemy groups. The term "terrorists" didn't mean anything in our battalion. It wasn't important.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, just bear with me one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You indicated that at some point in your career, you were an assistant commander for security, and I think Mr. Meek, my learned friend, had asked you some questions concerning your responsibilities in that capacity. Do you recall responding to questions put to you by Mr. Meek along those lines?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you also indicated that part of your function in that capacity was to refer certain matters to the battalion commander. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in more serious cases of infringement by soldiers, those matters would get reported to the commander of the brigade; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you, as the deputy commander of the battalion, ever come to learn of any investigation that was undertaken within the battalion concerning the events involving Orahovac on the 14th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you, in your capacity as deputy commander of the battalion, come to learn of any investigation that was undertaken at the brigade level concerning those same events?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. Probably there were some rumours going around about that, but I was not informed, and I'm not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you ever come to learn of any order issued by Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, the commander of your brigade, either investigating the events concerning Orahovac on the 14th or instigating any type of disciplinary action with respect to any soldier involved in those events?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of anything like that. Our battalion probably was not involved in that. Had it been, I might have been informed but I'm not aware of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Ristic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, to your question as to the investigation that was undertaken at the brigade level, the witness said he heard some rumours. Could you clarify that with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think you've heard the concern of His Honour. Can you tell us what rumours you heard in relation to an investigation being undertaken into the events concerning Orahovac on the 14th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I did not express myself well. I said there was no investigation in our battalion. Had there been I would have known about it. I was not involved down there. I didn't have any information. And it would not be appropriate for me to talk about things I may have heard about but I'm not really familiar with. I don't really know about them. I was tied to the battalion. I spent my time in the battalion. There was little talk of that and if I heard something but I don't have any firsthand knowledge or any reliable knowledge about those events, then I wouldn't like to talk about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ristic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, we don't have any further questions for you, which means you're free to go. Our staff will assist you. But before you leave this courtroom, on behalf of the Tribunal and the Trial Chamber, I should like to thank you for having come over to give evidence in this case, and on behalf of everyone, I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, documents? Do you wish to tender any documents from this witness, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We only wish to tender the document that was offered by Mr. Haynes. If he's not planning to tender it, then we will but other than that, there is nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's start with you, Mr. Bourgon, would you like to tender any documents? You've made use of some.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, good morning, colleagues. Mr. President, we would like to introduce into evidence 3D94, which is the map that was used by the witness but we would like to introduce the map without any markings because it might be used later on with other witnesses but also the map, the one that he marked, and those are the only documents we wish to tender into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, can you follow that? Okay. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I take it it's not the kind of documents that any of the other Defence teams would object to. So there being no objections, they are so admitted and they will be given a number by the registrar which will be communicated to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: A number of documents, please. P00348, that is the death certificate for Gojko Simic; 5 entries from the Zvornik Brigade duty officer's notebook, they are 7D159, 165, 166, 167 and 181; P00381 and P00382, those are the two documents setting out the brigade strength in terms of manpower and military hardware of the Zvornik Brigade; 7D362, which is the order of the 16th of July of 1993. I was originally going to invite you to mark that for identification purposes only because the translation is only provisional, but since Mr. Vanderpuye has put in P02405, the draft translation, I'd invite to you admit them both into evidence since there appears to be no contest about the accuracy of the translation. 7D363, which is the witness statement of Predrag Ilic that will have to be marked for identification purposes only because it is not translated to my knowledge; and lastly, the map as marked by the witness on the screen which as I understand the position should be called 7DIC86. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Haynes. Any objections, Mr. Vanderpuye? Could you incidentally address Mr. Haynes' suggestion that once you have made use of P02405, the draft translation, that should also be admitted? In other words, instead of having -- instead of having 7D362 marked for identification purposes, Mr. Haynes is suggesting that it is -- that it will be admitted on the basis that the draft, provisional and unofficial translation apparently is not contested by you, rather it has even been made use of by you. So on that basis, he suggests that they are both admitted and not marked for identification purposes. If I understood you well, Mr. Haynes, but I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, it seems to save time. It doesn't look like we are arguing about the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, the exhibit number P02405 is only a partial translation, a translation of part of that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I'm saying that that order should be translated later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I agree, and that's what I was about to articulate. I think for what it's worth it's okay but I think for the purposes of having an official translation of the entire document we need a translation of the entire thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. Any objection with that, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Not an objection, but it's been drawn to my attention that the document is in fact P02504, not 2405.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Registrar, please take note of this. Any objections to the admission of any of the documents that have been listed by Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Only I would suggest with respect to the duty officer logbook entries that, that the period from the 11th through the 23rd be admitted in order to -- in order to complete the picture of the entries that are being tendered and I don't know if Mr. Haynes has a particular objection to that but I think it would be a more useful -- it would be more useful to the Court to evaluate those entries in terms of their context within that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: At this point in time I'm only seeking the admission of the documents I used with this witness. The Prosecution will admit into evidence the duty officer's notebook in due course. When they do, they can do and I will have no objection at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that should be the position to be taken. And later on, if you wish to have other pages from that record to be introduced in evidence, you will have all the opportunity to do so. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Then I have no further objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So Madam Registrar, these documents that have been listed by Mr. Haynes are admitted. In relation to the translation of 7D362, we are told that there is a provisional translation of part of it. Whatever you made use of has to be substituted by a proper, official translation of the entire document. All right? Once you have done that, you will -- that will enter into the records and the other one will disappear, in other words. In other words, the one which you made use of today will remain marked for identification purposes, with the understanding that you will replace it with a full, official accepted translation. In that case, both that document and the original document in B/C/S that Mr. Haynes made use of, which are both -- which is also being marked for identification, will come into the records as fully admitted documents. All right? Agreed? Okay. Mr. Meek, you have no documents to tender? Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I think we can move to the next witness who I understand is a viva voce witness and he enjoys no protective measures; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's my understanding, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to confirm because situations change from day to day sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And from minute to minute. That's my understanding right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. President, just a matter regarding Witness 123. He was a witness that we had offered as 92 ter. We have confirmed that that witness has recently died so we will of course be withdrawing that application and we will be reviewing it for 92 quater and I owe you an estimate and everyone an estimate for the Prosecution's time period and I will have that for you tomorrow, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. You're about to start giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You're about to start giving evidence very soon. Before you do so, our rules require that you make a solemn undertaking with us that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Usher who is standing next to you will hand to you now the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Babic. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are first going to be asked questions by Mr. McCloskey, whom you've met already. He will then be followed by some of the Defence teams on cross-examination. I do not expect your testimony to finish today. Probably it will, if everyone cooperates, including yourself, we will finish it tomorrow. May I suggest to you that in answering questions you answer the question, the whole question and nothing but the question, please. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President I forgot to mention that I think as I've talked to the witness a caution is probably appropriate in the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, we have adopted a principle of justice in our rules, which is found throughout the world in most systems, namely we pay homage, we respect the right of a witness or of any person for that matter not to incriminate himself. For that purpose, we have provided a rule which basically provides that a witness may object to making any statement, and for that matter to answering any question put to him, which might tend to incriminate him. However, this is not an absolute rule. In case you are asked questions which, if answered, could lead to your possible incrimination, you can ask the Trial Chamber to give you permission not to answer such questions. We may decide in favour of your request, but we are also entitled not to grant your request and to order you to compel you to answer such questions. But there is a safeguard. In case we compel you, we order you, to answer such incriminatory questions, your testimony, your answer, compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in any subsequent prosecution that might be taken against you for any offence except if you are found responsible for false testimony. Is this clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I think on the basis of what I have been telling you, we may proceed with the examination-in-chief, and as I said, please expect to be here today and tomorrow. We'll try to finish with you tomorrow. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you first tell us for the record your full name?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. Aleksa Rajko Babic, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: The village of Krasanovici in Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: In the same village. I went to school in Bratunac, Srebrenica and later on in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your profession?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I was a teacher of Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us just a bit about your teaching career, where you taught, what years roughly, just a brief outline?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: From 1971 to 1986, in Pilica. Then for seven years in Zvornik. And in 1991, I returned to Pilica. And this is where I still work actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what school is that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: The Nikola Tesla primary school in Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that in or near the village of Kula?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: The village is Pilica, and Kula is a hamlet belonging to that bigger village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when the war broke out in 1992, what did you do? Were you assigned to the army?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: At the time, I worked at the Mitar Trifunovic Uco school in Zvornik and since the journey was no longer possible, I returned to Pilica. That same year, I was mobilised into the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you give us just another brief outline of what you did in the army and whether or not you went back to any school activities from 1992 up to 1995?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I started in the 1st Battalion. I was assistant commander for moral guidance. I returned to school in 1993, and I stayed up to 15 May 1994, and then I was mobilised into the battalion again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you were mobilised in 1994, what was your job?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I was assistant commander for general affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did that involve?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I was an officer for general affairs. That's the title. And it mostly involved accounting, administrative work, lists, paperwork, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clear up the record, you were not an assistant commander in 1994, you were a referent, an administrative clerk; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I was wrong when I said I was assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you hold that same position in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And at some point in July 1995, did -- were some Muslims transported to the area of Pilica?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what day was that, as far as you can remember? What was the date?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: 14 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the day? When you first woke up, what did you do? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I was on holiday. I'd been on holiday for three days. I was at home. In the morning, I was supposed to report to my unit. On that same day. On the 14th. In order to arrive there on time, I had to leave around 6.00, which I did. It took over an hour to the command post. It was hot so one had to make stops. I believe that I arrived at the unit sometime between 7.00 and 8.00. I did not consult my watch. And I reported to the unit. I let them know that I had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us what hamlet or village the unit headquarters was that you reported to?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Manojlovici is the hamlet and the village is Lokanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you reported it to the headquarters, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I was supposed to get ready, and I was told that I was supposed to be on duty on that day. We called those people duty officers. I was supposed to be duty officer, although I was not an officer, I was a foot soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I approached my colleague, who was sitting in the chair, normally occupied by the duty officer. He got up and he got ready to leave and to go to have rest, and I took his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you review any materials after that? Or did you receive any communications?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: It was our custom, when we arrived from holiday, to inspect the duty officer's log to see what had happened from the moment we left to the moment we came back from furlough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And tell us what happened as you began your duty shift.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: First, I read the entries in the logbook from the day when I was sent home, and I arrived at the last page that was filled out by my predecessor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you notice, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Of all the entries, of all the sentences, I remember one that I read. It was about a telegram entitled, "From the command of the Zvornik Brigade to the 1st Battalion." That was the title of the telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did it say?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I may not be correct in quoting exactly but I will give you the content: We are informing the command of the 1st Battalion that in the course of 14 of July, a group of anything between 100 and 200 men will arrive from Srebrenica at our battalion. We hereby order to the 1st Battalion to prepare the gym in the school near Kula. These people are to spend the night there and to be exchanged in Tuzla on the following day. Second, accesses should be provided to the school once these people are accommodated in the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you -- what do you mean by accesses should be provided? That's not real clear.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: There are two entrances to the school, the so-called main entrance and the auxiliary entrance and the meaning was once they enter the school, three or four soldiers should be placed at the main door and three or four soldiers should be placed at the auxiliary door in order to prevent anybody from -- anybody unauthorised from entering the school. This is what I meant, to secure the accesses to the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday, in my office, we spoke about this. You thought you may have actually received that report over the phone. Have you had a chance to think about that, on whether or not you might have received that report or that you actually read it in the duty officer notebook?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I read the book, the duty officer logbook, and it arrived in my office from another house where there was communication centre of our battalion. This centre received telegram and these telegrams are communicated by the phone to our office, and then we use the logbook or a piece of paper to record the content of the telegram communicated to us over the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you think you might have received this information you just told us about or had it been your previous duty officer?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I signed in my statement that I had found it there. I believe that this is correct. I stated that on the 13 and 14 March 2005, and I believe that my recollection was better then than it is now. So I would say that what I stated then was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And do you remember that notation in the logbook, could you tell or do you remember what date it had been received by the battalion?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: It was on the 14th of July of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know roughly what time of day you remember seeing this communication in the logbook?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Well, I arrived, as I've told you, between 7.00 and 8.00 in the morning. I suppose that I must have read that sometime between 8.00 and 9.00 or even between 7.00 and 9.00. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And was anything done there in the command that morning pursuant to that order in the logbook?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: The deputy commander was at the headquarters when I arrived, my predecessor, the security officer and the officer for moral guidance. Since the commander wasn't there, we set down around that desk in order to see what we could do pursuant to that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just, first of all, tell us the names of the people that had the positions you just told us about?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who was the -- who was the commander, for example?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: The deputy commander was Captain Momir Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was the commander?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: According to my information, he was being treated for a minor infection in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you said the security officer was there. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: The security officer was a non-commissioned officer of the former army, Tomislav Peric [as interpreted] and the officer for moral guidance was a foot soldier, Dragan Antic [as interpreted]. And Rajko Babic was an administrative officer, which is me. And the person called Jovan Rajic [as interpreted] was the duty officer from whom I had taken over. Did I mention everybody?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, the security officer's name, what was he known by?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: His nickname is a bit derogatory. I'd like to avoid using that nickname for the sake of the listeners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't need to know his nickname at this point what was his regular name because I'm not sure if we got it right in the record?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Okay. I can modify it a little. We called him Captain Muderiz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was his name Slavko Peric?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, Slavko Peric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the officer for moral guidance, was that Dragan Pantic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's a good place to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, we left off at the headquarters of the 1st Battalion. What did the small group you've described do? Or what did they decide to do? Can you tell us about what happened then?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: After discussion and a conversation, we decided that all those who happened to be there at the headquarters, save for the deputy commander, Pelemis, to head towards the school in Pilica, and that the group should be joined by a signalsman, a guard, a logistics man and a few soldiers who would be able to carry out the task of securing the school in Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did that happen?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: This is exactly what we did but there was another option, to supplement our group, on the road leading from our headquarters to the school, any soldier en route to the position, we could order that soldier not to go to the combat lines that night but to join us and to increase our strength around the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So when you got to the school, about how many soldiers did you have there for security?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Together with me, there were 12 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And again, which of the -- was Slavko Peric with you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: He was one of the 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was anyone in charge of your group?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: While we were still in the command, we agreed it should be Slavko Peric because he was the most senior among us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And how about the morale officer, Dragan Pantic? Did he go to the school as well?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you all do when you got to the school there at Kula?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: We divided into three groups of four. One group of four soldiers went to the schoolyard to secure the auxiliary entrance. The second group of four men remained near the main entrance, to control entry into the school. Dragan Pantic, Slavko, another man and I, I don't remember who, went inside the school. Our task was to go to the gym to see what condition it was in, to see if there was anything that had to be taken out of it and moved to other rooms, to see whether one could leave without any obstacles, to see whether there was any gym equipment that might cause a hazard, and remove it. And that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you just tell us what happened after you got it set up?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: When we had done all this, we were on our way out of the gym and from the door to the gym to the door to the school, the distance is 2 or 3 metres approximately like the distance between me and the gentleman. When I turned the corner, going towards the door, I was surprised to see an armed soldier standing at the door who was not from my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you see then?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I looked through the glass door and the window, and I noticed on the path leading up to the school, two or three civilians walking towards the school with their hands behind their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you have an idea who these civilians were?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I've already said that we knew that -- well, we knew from the order, I've told you about before, that they were from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so can you tell us what happened, what you saw, that day after this?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: We stood behind the soldier at the door, three or four metres away, and he asked me where the gym was in the school. I pointed in the direction of the gym, which was to his right, and I stood there in the middle of the corridor together with Pantic, Slavko, and he ordered that the civilians should enter one by one and proceed to the gym, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just keep describing what you saw. How many -- how many civilians did you see enter the gym?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Very well. The civilians came in one by one, two or three metres apart from each other, so that on the path leading up to the school you could see three or four of them at any one time. They passed by and I always thought there were no more civilians because there would be periods when no civilians were coming, but then some minutes or seconds after that, another group of civilians would appear in the same way, with their hands behind their heads, and so it went on in the same way and it was very hard for us to control the numbers. Some walked faster, some walked more slowly. We found ourselves surprised, a little bit confused. I tried to count them but I lost count. So I stopped counting. But they came in waves, with interruptions, and so it went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly about what time of day these first Muslims started arriving at the school?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I tried to establish that. I went to the command where I spent three or four hours. Then I went back. I set up the gym. And in my view, it might have been after 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. After 1400 hours, when the Muslims first started arriving at that school?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us roughly, your best estimate, of how long Muslims continued to arrive?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Do you mean how many or do you mean for how long?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's start with how long. How long were they arriving, as best as you can estimate?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I think that the entry into the gym lasted at least 30, up to perhaps 50, minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you get any idea of the number that -- the total number after they'd all arrived?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: It was very hard even to guess. So I went to the gym a little later to see what this looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you see?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: In the gym, I saw a lot of people, and they took up about two-thirds of the gym space. If you know what a basketball field is like, they were up to the first racket near the entrance door, some five metres. That was the area that was not full. Some were squatting, some were standing up, some were sitting. It was very hard to estimate the numbers because they were in different positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And aside from the -- what you've described as the 12 men from the 1st Battalion, how many men from this unit that you didn't know were in -- did you see around the school that day?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I was inside the school. As I said, you can only see about 10 metres up to the corner. In the area I was able to see, together with the two or three who were inside, there were two or three outside directing the civilians, so they wouldn't go off in another direction towards where I lived, for example, so I saw three to five of them. I don't know whether they changed shifts. I don't know whether there were any others nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever find out where these soldiers that you didn't know were from?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe that, it's still that first day, the 14th, what happened after all the Muslims became loaded into the gym? Just give us the outline of the events as you recall them.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: When the soldier who directed the civilians into the gym went to the gym, he probably saw that the gym couldn't hold any more civilians. He went back to his position at the door and told the others who were outside that no more civilians could be taken to the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Then the two who were with him stood at the main door. The gym door remained open so you could always see the civilians. And they stood guard there. They remained there. The soldier at the door was already free to leave. He stood there chatting to us. He asked where the toilet was. He asked whether he could have a drink of water. And we stood there because we didn't dare go to the gym right away to take a look. I asked him, "Can we go and see?" I asked if I could go and see what was happening in the gym, and he permitted it. I went up to the -- to one of the two doors leading from the gym to the parking place. And I saw those Muslims who were taking up two-thirds of the gym space. And then I returned to the corridor. The guards continued standing guard. They changed from time to time. And now something happened that we had not foreseen or known about. Outside, the temperature was about 30 degrees Centigrade. There were no windows open in the gym and there was no ventilation. The civilians were sweaty when they arrived, or wet or unkempt or unwashed. And I felt a terrible smell emanating from the gym. And it was becoming more and more unbearable. The guards started complaining that they couldn't stand at the door. They kept asking for replacements. So that every three or four minutes we had to change the guards. In the meantime, things became even worse. The windows in the corridors began to mist up and you couldn't see through them. You could hear the rumour of voices from the gym and I could see them approaching our guard getting closer and closer to him. When they were sitting in the gym, the guard was perhaps 25 metres away from them in the corridor, but at one point they had already come to his feet, they were squatting there. They were asking us to let them go out, refresh themselves, get some water, go to the toilet. I spoke to my men and we agreed, because we had two buckets of water, two barrels of about 200 litres each in the bathroom. We allowed three or four civilians, accompanied by a guard, to help us carry those barrels to the corridor near the door leading into the gym. We thought we could let them get out of the gym one by one and refresh themselves and then go back. But every civilian, every prisoner who left the gym, he would splash his comrade, not himself, with water. They would splash each other with water. And very soon, there was a large puddle around these buckets and the water was evaporating and causing even more mist on the windows. But that would not have been a problem if they had wanted to go back to the gym, those men. But they would stand by the barrel. Others would approach it and suddenly there were so many of them around the barrel that I had the impression half of them were there. There were two steps in the corridor and they sat there and then there was a staircase leading upstairs, which in length is perhaps from here to that door, and they started sitting on those steps and we couldn't prevent them from doing that. We didn't want to issue any orders. And the soldier at the door didn't try to make them go back into the gym because it seems that he himself felt that they couldn't go back there because of the smell and the bad air. Some of the men collapsed. I didn't see any actually faint or lose consciousness, but they were all sweaty, they had taken off their T shirts, they splashed each other with water, and at one point they were all out of the gym, there was not a single one left in the gym. And the hallway, the lobby, together with the stairs was a much bigger space, and now the windows could be opened and when they were sitting in the corridor and on that staircase, our guards and I, and our men, had a problem because we couldn't control them any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me one second. Under our rules we need to try to go question and answer and I don't want to interrupt your story because it will make it more difficult, I think, but let's try to go a little more step by step.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: You told me -- it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've been fine. So with this problem you've described, where were the Muslims allowed to -- or where were they moved to?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Now they were all in the corridor. The soldier who had the role of issuing orders asked us what the classrooms upstairs were like. He asked me if I would accompany him to take a look at the classrooms. I couldn't refuse, and I didn't mind going with him. So I did. Through the rows of prisoners sitting on the staircase, and upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The soldier that had the role of issuing orders, was that one of the soldiers you didn't know or was that a member of the 1st Battalion?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: It was one of those I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: We went upstairs. Upstairs, there were six classrooms. Of the six, one was not in use. It wasn't open, because there were computers in it and that was always kept under lock and key. As the school was closed for the summer, that room was closed and one of the teachers had the key. We looked at one classroom. He looked at the windows and the -- how high they were from the pavement outside, and he said all right. I had to show him another one. He said it was all right. Then the third and the fourth and the fifth and he was satisfied. Then he went back to those Muslims who were already on the steps, they were all the way up to the landing, and they were talking among themselves, so he got them to be quiet and he told them to go to the classroom on his right, one by one, and they obeyed him. He looked to see how many could fit in and when he established no more could fit in, he told them to go to the second classroom. And they obeyed and so it went on until all the classrooms were full and not a single Muslim was left outside in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were Muslims allowed to receive or go get water?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: As the barrels were downstairs, and the water in them was already dirty, I remembered that in the school they had some containers for carrying bread or rolls to the pupils, and you could -- they could hold some 15 litres of water. They had handles. So I went to the door of each classroom and told those Muslims if they wanted water to drink, they should choose among themselves two men for each classroom and I found those containers in the school kitchen. There were 12 of them. So I gave two to each classroom. I told them to take those containers and escorted by our soldier to go to a spring which was some 70 or 80 metres away from the school, to fill them with fresh water and escorted by the soldier, to bring the water to the classroom, in front of the classroom, and they did that very nicely. So that each classroom had two of those containers full of water and they were very happy about that. I told them to open up the way so that those who needed it most could approach those containers and take water and that's what they did. A similar situation obtained when they wanted to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was this spring, more precisely in relation to the school?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Near the auxiliary door -- entrance, there is a playing field, a sports field, some 15 metres, then there is a small slope some 30 or 40 metres so altogether it's about 70 metres below the school. There is a pathway leading to that spring. There is a fountain that has been built there. That water was used for the school. But as there was no more electricity, there was no running water in the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did anything -- did you learn that anything happened to any Muslim that went to get water that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: While I was in the corridor at one point I heard at the auxiliary door that there was some kind of commotion. When I approached to see what was going on because there was nothing else for me to do, I was just standing there, I found that one Muslim had rolled up his trouser leg on his right leg, his right side was facing me, he was holding his leg and shouting, "I'm wounded." He probably went to get water with his brother, the young man was holding him up. He wasn't lying down. He was standing there. There wasn't even any bleeding from the wound. And he said, "Hold on, brother. You're the only one left. Hold up, if we could only reach Tuzla tomorrow." I looked at the wound. We didn't have anything to dress it with. There was no blood running from it. That young man took off his T-shirt and bandaged up the wound and then they went to the classroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of wound was it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: It was an exit-entry wound below the knee through the muscle. I don't know what the name of the muscle is. In the back of the leg, underneath the knee. It wasn't the bone that was damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did any of the people there tell you how he had received that wound and --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: He told me. I asked him what happened. And he said, "They wounded me." And I said, "What did you do?" And he said, "I started to flee." And I said, "Why did you do that, for heaven's sake?" And he said, "They were shooting." And I said, "Well, were they shooting at you?" And he said, "No, but I got scared and I started running." And then probably our soldiers prevented him from escaping and shooting at him as he was fleeing, they probably hit him in the leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear any shooting outside the school that afternoon and evening?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: You could hear shooting around the school every day. There were two or three shops there and our men on their way back from the duty stops would go and drink there until late at night. Once they got really drunk, they would shoot into the air so that hearing the sound of shooting was nothing unusual. I was inside. There was a lot of noise inside. The people were calm but they talked among themselves and it echoed in the school and you couldn't hear anything else. And also, I was so used to hearing the sound of shooting I didn't pay any attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About what time of day did this person come with the bullet wound? Or when did you see him with the bullet wound? About what time of day?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: It was when they went up there to the classrooms. I don't know when. I can't remember. It was in the afternoon but I don't know exactly when. The time had stopped for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you stay there when it got dark?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened, if anything, that night?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Nothing interesting happened save for the fact that we experienced a light outage, an electricity outage. The prisoners took that opportunity to come down the stairs and they tried to go for a walk. It was dark. We could not recognise each other let alone the Muslims. We reflected on what to do. I remembered that in my apartment I had three or four candles that I had brought from the positions. I had brought them to my wife to have when there was no electricity. At the time, candles were hard to get by. I left and went to my apartment and in my apartment where I hadn't been for two or three years before that, I managed to find three or four candles. I brought them to the school and I placed them along the staircase, and I lit them, which enabled us to control the people who were going up and down the stairs. And the night continued. Nothing new happened. They went to the toilet, they went to get a sip of water, they were calm. Our guards did not have any need to control them. The windows were open. There was a light breeze. It was not hot. And they were even grateful to us, when I spoke to them, that they felt comfortable actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you sleep at all that night at the school?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: No, I did not sleep at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was Slavko Peric with you at the school that night?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Dragan Pantic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the next morning, what happened the next morning?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Before Slavko Peric left home that evening, we had agreed that he should go to the battalion command or the brigade command and to ask for our replacement. It seemed that nobody would come to fetch these people the following day so we sent him to spend the night at home, to go to the brigade the following morning, to see what would become of these men, if they were not to be taken anywhere and to give us reinforcement because the 12 of us had already been exhausted from the long night, and Slavko left, we the rest of us stayed behind, awaiting what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in the morning when it became light, what happened?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Nothing. We were just standing there in our positions. They did whatever they were supposed to do, toilet, water. They were in the classrooms. I inspected the classrooms. I talked to them. They asked me things. I would answer if I knew what to tell them. I even hoped that I would bump into some people I knew from Srebrenica and that somebody might recognise me. They started addressing me as "principal," and they told me, "Don't fret. We will be calm. Today we will be exchanged," as if they had noticed that the four of us were actually afraid for our lives because they outnumbered them and they could have attacked us. That's how I proceeded. I calmed down. I told them if they behaved, we would behave. They listened to that voice of reason and nothing happened. While they were there nothing bad happened to them. Everybody behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you relieved that day sometime?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: When Slavko brought people who would replace the 12 of us, I believe that he brought more soldiers. I couldn't check how many because the four didn't go home, the other four or us, we didn't go home. The new soldiers just replaced us and I could go to the staff room to sit down, if there was coffee, I could have a drink of coffee. And the other three were in the school, in my stead, and instead of the others. Those soldiers who were standing guard were taking a nap on the staircase, if they could, but nobody went home. So the number of soldiers and the number of us inside went up. This lasted for some hour or so and then, when I realised and when I got Slavko's permission to do so, I went to my apartment to get some rest. But I didn't enter my apartment. I entered another apartment, an apartment facing the school because it was all the same, which apartment you entered. They were all accessible. The doors were wide open. There were a few of my soldiers there taking a nap on one of the couches. I sat down on one of the couches. I tried to stay awake but I couldn't. I fell asleep. I woke up and it was already night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me take you back a little bit. You had mentioned that on the 14th, you'd gone over to the school with about eight soldiers from the 1st Battalion. When Slavko came back on the 15th with more soldiers, what happened to those original eight? Were they allowed to leave or did they stay at the school?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I've just told you they stayed, all together, but they did not stand guard. They were not on duty. They could go and have a rest in the garden. They could relax. They could be at ease. They could lie down on the grass. So they were not on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And roughly how many soldiers did Slavko bring back with him?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I never asked him that. At least 20, I would say.
