utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Plus the 12 would make up a total number of anything between 40 and 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What unit were the 20 that he brought from?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: My unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That's the 1st Battalion?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So tell us what the next thing you remember happening at the school is. You fell asleep on that -- on the 15th and you woke up that night and the prisoners were still there. Where did you sleep the night of the 15th, morning of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I spent that night in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And morning of the 16th, what did you see? What happened?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I had decided not to go there any more because I did not intend to stand guard any more. I wanted to avoid that. I was observing from my terrace actually from a window facing the school door, and I could only see what was going on in front of the door. I couldn't see what was going on inside the school. I also spoke with a soldier who was walking by the building as I was standing on the terrace, I asked him if anything had happened. He said nothing was going on. You asked me about the 16th? Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The morning of the 16th.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: And at one point I noticed in front of the school door, in front of the right wall, I saw three Muslims standing next to each other facing the wall, and I couldn't see immediately how many more were standing closer to the school, but later on I heard that they exited the school in groups of eight. Then they would face the wall. The other eight that followed them escorted by the other soldiers, they would tie their soldier -- their soldiers' hands behind their back and they would blindfold them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see this blindfolding process or did you just hear about it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I saw the three. I could only see the three. The view of the others was blocked by the wall but I assume the others were also blindfolded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. McCloskey, because this is not clear to me. Previous page, page 46, lines 22, 23 and 24: "The other eight that followed them escorted by the other soldiers, they would tie their soldier -- their soldiers' hands behind their back and they would blindfold them." The soldiers' hands is a little bit confusing, if you could clarify that with a witness, please. It could be a question of interpretation, too, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell us who was tying up who?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: The other eight Muslims would tie the hands of the previous eight Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Were there any soldiers around them while they were doing this?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: The other soldiers, two or three of them, would be standing behind the backs of the group of eight who would be tying the hands of the first group. They would be standing behind their backs while this was being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And again, roughly, what time of day did you see this tying process happen on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was between 10.00 and 11.00, if my memory serves me well. It was a summer day. It was hot. I don't know. In any case, it was before the noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any vehicles come?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I personally did not see any vehicle coming. I suppose that at the time I was in the other part of the apartment. But from my apartment I saw, in the playground, I saw the back half of a parked bus. I could only see one half of the bus. I couldn't see the front half of the bus. And that was the only vehicle I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any people around the bus or anybody put in the vehicle -- the bus?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I didn't see the front door of the bus, and this is the door that they probably used to enter the bus. They didn't use the back door. And I only could see the back door. I couldn't see the front door. There was nobody around the bus, around the part of the bus that I could observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you receive any information that Muslims were kept in any area outside the school, around the village?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you get any word that Muslims were in buses or vehicles?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: When they stopped entering the gym, at that moment I suppose that some of them remained on the road in the buses or in some other vehicles. I don't know what kind of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you get any information to that effect that day, that first day, the 14th, that there were Muslims in vehicles?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Well, only when everything was over, the villagers who had their houses around the school told me that there were at least six buses who had brought those Muslims over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you see any senior officer or officers around the school during these days, 14, 15 or 16?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anybody on the 14th. On the 15th, sometime in the afternoon, somebody came and I didn't know that he was an officer until I heard people addressing him as Colonel, Lieutenant Colonel. I noticed him at the moment when he was sitting in front of the apartment where I had spent the night. He was sitting on a pile of fuel wood, and our soldiers who had stood guard were around him. I don't know whether there were any other soldiers with him. I don't know. I didn't see him come. I approached that group. My men said, "Teacher, this is a colonel, a high-ranking officer." They whispered to me that I should behave and that I should watch my mouth. When I heard that a higher-ranking officer was here who could issue orders, I approached him, I greeted him, but I didn't dare ask his name or anything else. He greeted me very politely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me interrupt right there. You had mentioned that you'd seen an officer and then you mentioned Lieutenant Colonel, Colonel, and then you said people said there is a colonel there. Do you know was it a lieutenant colonel or a colonel, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. He did not have any patches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after he greeted you politely, what happened or what was said?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I asked him what should be done with the people in the school. We were very interested in that, because we had been given a very tall order. Our unit was composed of farmers and we had to deal with the issue of such a great number of people. We were not prepared. We were not skilled. And we could hardly wait for somebody to appear to tell us what to do with these people, what would happen of them, so that we could go back to our unit and that our obligation towards those people could stop. I wanted to rejoin my unit. I wanted to lock the school and go back to the usual business. He said, "Listen, sir, you are a farmer's unit, a battalion. We have brought Muslims to you and you don't know how to take them away." I suppose that he meant that we were to take them to Tuzla to be exchanged. And then I asked him how am I supposed to take them? And what escort? And where should I take them? Answer: He says, "Well, you are good for nothing."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did he say anything about what was -- might happen to these-- or what was going to happen to these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: In the course of that first day and the second day, I went to a classroom where the Muslims -- some Muslims said that they knew me. The soldiers who guarded them told me that. They told me, "Teacher, they want to see you in the classroom number 4. They have recognised you." I was actually glad to be recognised by somebody. I went there immediately to the door of that classroom. I was standing at the door, and I asked people if anybody knew me. First, they looked me with -- at me with mistrust, and then a hand was raised in a corner, next to the window, and in the middle of a row, in the last bench, another hand went up, and they were very close to each other, just a passage separated them. They were as close to each other as I am with this gentleman. The one next to the window was a tall, blond guy. He introduced himself as a Muslim. His family name sounded very long. I knew exactly what village he was from. And he told me, when I asked him how he knew me, he told me, "I have your photo in my house. And your entire football team." Because I had played football and his village had also had a football club and we competed against each other. Once we played a game in his village, and our photo was taken, it was copied and distributed among the players. I am from Bratunac. He was also from Bratunac. And he also knew my brother in Bratunac, as well as myself. That's why he raised his hand and he said he knew me. And the other one who raised his hand, he told me that his name was Zoran. I couldn't remember him. He had dark hair. He was very tall, very strong, he could have easily carried me in his arms. He only told me that his name was Zoran. I didn't ask him anything else but I asked the Muslims who were squatting in that classroom to let me through to get to the two of them. And they could both reach me with their hands. I had a military overall and I had pockets, and in every pocket I had a pack of cigarettes. I didn't want the other soldier to hear me. I whispered to the two of them, "Take the cigarettes from my pockets. This is all I can give you." I asked them if they were hungry and they said that they did and I told them that I had only one loaf of bread at home and they said, "Thank you very much. Don't bring it to us because we will kill each other over it and thank you very much for the cigarettes." And this was the end of our conversation. Now, let me tell you what I asked the colonel. I asked if any Muslims would stay or whether they would all be taken from Pilica, whether we could keep at least one or two of them, and they he shouted at me, "No, they can't stay, they had to be taken away, all of them. I don't want to talk to you any more." I turned around and I left and I never saw him again after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What if anything did you understand that to mean, what the colonel told you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I realised that nothing good would happen to those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember what you told the investigator back in September?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I believe that I said that the thought that occurred to me at the moment was that they would all be killed. I suppose that I said something to that effect. And then I decided I would never set foot in the school until it was empty and I never went there again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us an accurate description of this lieutenant colonel or colonel, as I know you gave us a description back -- let me finish the date, September 2005, when you talked to an investigator. Can you -- can you describe this colonel or lieutenant colonel? And if you need to look at the report to help refresh your recollection, that's fine, but we would like to get your best recollection as you sit here. If you can.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I can remember but I don't know how my description started. So if I don't follow the same order, please don't hold it against me. The hair was blond, fair. He was rather tall. The hair was not thick. It was very short in the back. And the hair was receding and that's why the hair was parted to one side, to cover that receding hairline. The person was strong, heavily built. He had the military appearance. I don't know what else. I believe that my previous description was, similar to what I've just given you, he wore a camouflage uniform. His sleeves were rolled up so he looked even more muscular, stronger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember any facial hair?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: He was neatly shaved, and he sweated profusely. It was very hot. He was very neatly shaved and he did not sport a mustache.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. At some point, did you go back to the battalion command and look in the logbook?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: When the school was empty, I took my things and I went back to the unit because my task of securing the school was over. I arrived at the unit because I had been absent for three days, and it was planned for me to be absent just one day. I reported up there, and I wanted to check the logbook because that was the custom, as I have told you, to see what had happened while one was away. And I was surprised not to find that page containing the order. It wasn't there. It was missing from the logbook. And nobody wanted to tell me how it had gone missing or why. If somebody had told me how it had gone missing, he would have also had to tell me why it had gone missing. So it has remained unclear why and how this page went missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Babic. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have on our list all the Defence teams barring the Borovcanin one who wish to cross-examine this witness. Is the situation still the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are very unlikely to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And I have the Beara team indicating that they wish to -- they need one hour to cross-examine this witness. Have you arranged among yourselves who is going first basically? I'm starting with Beara, the Beara Defence team because they need the most time but if you want to start before Mr. Zivanovic you're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I start first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Mr. Zivanovic is appearing for Mr. Nikolic in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, for Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, for Mr. Popovic in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to put just a few questions to you. When asked by the Prosecutor about the civilians who were brought on that occasion, you mentioned something more than once. You called these prisoners "civilians". Could you clarify whether you called them civilians because they were wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was another thing I wanted to ask. You said that when you looked into the gym, about two-thirds of the gym was filled. You explained that it went up to some sort of racket. I'll show you some pictures later but what I want to know now is the following: When later you looked at the prisoners in the gym, can you confirm that no new prisoners were brought in?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at a photograph, it's our 1D01276.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could show the photos on the ELMO, which might be more practical and the witness could mark them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you recognise this hall?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the gym in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether this photograph was taken from the entrance?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it taken from the corner parallel to the wall?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Well, give me a minute to take a look. Could I have a better look at this part on the wall?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe you could look at the photograph directly. It's to your right.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: This was taken from the door, the entry, the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark approximately on this photograph the place up to which the gym was filled with prisoners, as you described? I think you have -- it might be better if you were to look at the photograph rather than the monitor.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Can I take it? You see here where this vertical line is, that's the centre of the gym. And if you look at the bottom part, this bottom part was not filled, this bottom part, if you turn the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have a marker there. Could you just mark what you just explained?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Well, the other side -- I need to mark the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, choose the picture you want.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Well, you can't see up to where they reached in this photograph. You can't see the racket and they were next to the racket.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the other three photographs and choose the one that is most suitable for this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Zivanovic, we have that picture on e-court. Would it not be more convenient for the witness to mark on this picture on the e-court? Thank you. I was mistaken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can mark it on this photograph here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Take a look now.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I can use this one too. [Marks] Enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So where you put this red mark.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, parallel to this white line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mark it, just feel free, draw a line.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Like this. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put your initials there?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the date?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Today is the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May I ask you now to mark this from another angle on the other photograph?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is now taken from the door.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put the date and your initials here?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, looking at this picture now, you have some experience in this, you can, for example, estimate the number of children in a classroom or in a gym. You don't have to count them in order to say how many there are. Can you say now that 1200 men could fit into this space?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: No, they couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Who is going next?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know it's a little early for a break but we may not have any questions at all so I'd like to consult with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We can have the break or we can start with someone else. I have the Pandurevic Defence, or Madam Fauveau for General Miletic. Go ahead. You requested 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we won't have any questions for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Nikolic have requested 45 minutes. So I would rather have them go the 45 minutes at a stretch. Yes, Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it will be less if we could consult our client. In view of Mr. Meek's suggestion, I think this might be a very good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless the Gvero team wishes to go. You requested ten minutes and we have got about 17 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can now confirm that we don't have any questions. As I indicated just before my learned friend Mr. Zivanovic began his cross-examination, we were unlikely to at that point. I'm sure we don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes or Mr. Sarapa? You requested 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Approximately 30 to 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa, is it convenient for you to start now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you said, please? Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could have a break, then after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll have a 25-minute break now, instead of at 12.30 and we will resume at 20 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So who is going to update us? Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, is it not correct that this supposed lieutenant colonel or colonel that you have described to the OTP and today did not wear spectacles and this is consistent with the statement you gave the OTP?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: No. He did not wear spectacles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, when you gave your statement to the OTP on the 13th and 14th of September 2005, you were shown a multitude of pictures?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And isn't it true, sir, that you did not -- that excuse me, that in those photographs, none of them depicted the person that you saw at the school on that day?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It's a double negative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is a double negative but I understood. If you want to clarify it with him, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I would clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's worth clarifying but it's understandable as it is, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let me clarify it, real quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, did you in all of the pictures you looked at with the Prosecutor back in 2005, less than two years ago, recognise in any of those photographs the supposed colonel or lieutenant colonel that you've described?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I will have only a few questions for you in connection with your testimony of today.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You talked about the situation in the school and that throughout those days, especially the 14th and 15th, you spent all your time in the school.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Trying to keep order there, together with the soldiers from your battalion?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It was your concern that everything should proceed calmly and peacefully and to help the people as to the best of your ability; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I understood from your testimony that there were soldiers present in the school whom you did not know?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And it was they for the most part who issued orders to all of you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would now like to go back to the telegram you received on the 14th of July 1995 in your battalion command. You paraphrased the text of the telegram, and as I understood it, it stated explicitly that all the people who arrived would be exchanged on the following day.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you yourself thought they would be exchanged on the 14th and 15th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of July, in the afternoon, as you testified today, your group of soldiers was replaced by another group of soldiers from the battalion?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They were brought by Mr. Peric and they were about 20 men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After this change of shift, nothing bad happened to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would now like to go back to another segment of your testimony, on page 54, lines 18 and 19, where, in response to a question by my colleague Mr. Zivanovic, you said that you thought these men were civilians because they were all wearing civilian clothes, ordinary clothes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that there were no women or children among them?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And they were grown men fit for military service?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, they were not all fit for military service. There were a few elderly men among them, if one considers them unfit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown several photographs when you were interviewed by the investigators of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you recognised some officers from the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You knew Mr. Drago Nikolic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Throughout those days, did you ever see Mr. Drago Nikolic in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And one last question: The soldiers whom you did not know, would you agree with me that they were neither members of your battalion or of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure they weren't members of my battalion but I don't know about the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic. That leaves us with Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that the first line of the 1st Battalion was around 7 kilometres if you go on foot or 20 kilometres if you go by car?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Obviously from the school in Pilica, the school where you were, from Pilica?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I did not hear the first word you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: The first line of the 1st Battalion was some seven kilometres if you go on foot or some 20 kilometres if you go by car from Pilica?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: The school in Pilica was a civilian facility?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Did it work throughout?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Would you agree that this school was never used by the 1st Battalion or the army?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Since you worked in the school, you were a teacher in that same school, and you reside in the area, you were very familiar with the outlay of the rooms in the school; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: The message that you read on the 14th in the logbook spoke about the arrival of some 100 to 200 people. Would you agree with the statement that this was the number of men that you saw in the gym and later on in the classrooms?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: One could say that there were somewhat more of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: How many approximately?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: At least 50 over 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So we are talking up to 250 people?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 14th, when you arrived in the school from the battalion, were you armed or not?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: I never wore arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: As you were leaving the battalion to go to the school, once you had read the message and decided to go together with the colleagues and the soldiers that you came across on the way, would you agree that the purpose of your arrival and the basic purpose of your being there was to provide security for those prisoners so as to provide for their fair safe exchange as it was indicated in the message that you had read out?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Was it also to provide security for the villagers in case one of the prisoners decided to escape?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: When you arrived at the school, was the school open, was it unlocked?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you know who unlocked the door?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you know who had the key?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you know or do you assume who was it who unlocked the door?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: The key must have been held by one of the three janitors. That's why I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So you assume?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, one of the three.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: But you don't know which one of them opened the school?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: You spoke about a colonel or lieutenant colonel or an officer of a high rank who arrived and with whom you had a brief conversation. Did any one of you from the battalion command recognise that person? Did any one of you knew him, his name or his rank?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BABIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Sarapa. I just want to confirm with the Borovcanin, Gvero and Miletic teams that you have no questions. All right. Do you have a re-examination, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no further questions for you, sir. I was wrong when I anticipated that you would be here testifying tomorrow as well. Basically that means that you are free to go. Our staff will assist you and facilitate your return back home at the earliest. On behalf of my colleagues on the Trial Chamber and on also the Tribunal, I wish to thank you are for having come over to give testimony and also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the direct examination and cross were so efficient, you might have noticed we accelerated several hours ahead of our schedule. We have a witness here but he hasn't been spoken to yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And I suppose that will happen between today and tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's happening right now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So, documents? Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender two photos I showed. And it is sent to registrar who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. That would be documented already. Any objections from the Prosecution or any of the Defence teams? None. So those two photos marked by the witness will -- are being admitted in evidence as the Defence, Popovic Defence team, exhibits. Do you wish to tender also the unmarked one or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it is necessary either. Anyway, I do appreciate that you've been caught in this situation. I suppose we can do nothing except if there are any issues that you would like to address the Chamber upon, perhaps you could do it now. We have got 45 minutes. I see Mr. Ostojic tempted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Only because of the statement made by my learned friend that he can enlighten us tomorrow on what the presumed schedule is for the remainder of the OTP case. I'm not sure if he's prepared or if he needed to evaluate it but I know that he thought a witness was coming and that maybe given the witness we didn't want to delay that witness, and perhaps he can share with us if he has that estimate and what that estimate may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I took it -- thank you, Mr. Ostojic. I took it that you were filing this tomorrow, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. I wanted to get my witness done first so I can focus on the work that the team has been putting together in that respect. So tomorrow, I should have better numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there anyone else who would like -- yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. During the testimony of not this witness but the previous witness, Mr. Ristic, an issue came about about two names that were mentioned by the Prosecution. One of those was Risto Trifkovic and the second one was I believe, Vojo Matic and the Prosecution said at that time that information had been disclosed to us and my colleague was right, this information was indeed disclosed to us on -- in February of 2007. So just recently. But it was disclosed to us -- simply a list of names was given to us on a CD and this in this particular case, it was an interview with two languages where you just cannot make out at all what was in English. I would appreciate, Mr. President, if the Prosecution could, when they do disclose information to us, at least tell us if it's something that will be used with a future witness, and give us either a paper copy or something that we can read because it could have been that this name could have been essential to the testimony of this witness. It turned out it wasn't. But it is important for us to get that information in advance and in this case, although they did give it to us we can't complain about that, we have no idea that this was going to be used with this witness, the name was never put to the witness in proofing, as was asked by the Trial Chamber and we were caught by surprise. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey, do you wish to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We endeavour to when we provide this discovery to give it in a written outline form so that you can look immediately, see who the person is and we'll continue to do that and if I can add what unit they are from and -- you know, I can try to beef that up so that there is -- so it's clear. But there was a very, you can could see, a very simple exercise to just to confirm that there was a person named Risto and Vojo in that unit, and -- but I can -- I do want to be able to give the Defence things that they can make sense out of and we'll continue to try to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Any further matters you would like to raise? Otherwise, we adjourn. Now, tomorrow, as you may have found out from the intranet news, I need to be away on official business so I will be here only for the first session. After that, we'll continue pursuant to 15 bis. I was suggesting, but I need a confirmation, if instead of having the break at 10.30, we could have the break at 10.45 or maybe somewhere near 11.00, I know it wouldn't be a problem for you but this is of concern mostly to interpreters and technicians and the rest of the staff. So if you can give us an indication -- you don't need to feed me back now or feed us back now. I mean, we -- you can confirm to us tomorrow morning. So we stand adjourned until tomorrow morning and we start with a new witness and then I won't be here on Friday. It's the same situation. I will return on Friday when the sitting is almost finished and by the time I get to The Hague, it will be over. So thank you and good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 19th day of April, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.05 p.m.,
